Pneumothorax on chest radiographs: 5

A large right-sided pneumothorax is associated with pressure effect and displacement of the central thoracic structures. Which direction of mediastinal movement fits an expanding pressurized right hemithorax rather than volume loss from right-lung collapse?

  1. Mediastinal displacement away from the pressurized hemithorax
  2. Visceral pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings
  3. Deep sulcus sign
  4. Immediate clinical treatment of suspected tension pneumothorax
  5. Skin-fold artifact
Answer and explanation

Mediastinal displacement away from the pressurized hemithorax

Pressure from a large or tension pneumothorax can push mediastinal structures contralaterally; clinical instability determines urgency.

Option explanations

Mediastinal displacement away from the pressurized hemithorax: Pressure from a large or tension pneumothorax can push mediastinal structures contralaterally; clinical instability determines urgency.

Visceral pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings: Pleural air separates the visceral pleura from the chest wall, leaving no lung vessels peripheral to the true pleural line. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Deep sulcus sign: In a supine patient, pleural air can collect anterobasally and make a costophrenic sulcus unusually deep and lucent. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Immediate clinical treatment of suspected tension pneumothorax: An unstable patient with a convincing tension pattern needs urgent decompression by a trained team; imaging must not delay treatment. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Skin-fold artifact: A skin fold can mimic a pleural line, but visible pulmonary markings beyond the apparent edge favor an artifact. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
